issues.failure_explanation: The lemma claims G(∞)=0 iff C+D=0, justified only by the asymptotic G(z) ~ (C+D)/(C−D/2), which requires C−D/2 ≠ 0. The point (C,D)=(0,0) belongs to the admissible parameter family of (Coefficient_2) and is never excluded. There the numerator 1+z[(1/6)+(2/3)R(z)] tends to 1+(5/6)z (since R(z)→1) while the denominator 1−z/6 tends to −z/6, so the true limit is G(∞) = (5/6)/(−1/6) = −5 ≠ 0. Hence C+D=0 holds but G(∞)≠0: the 'if' direction of the stated equivalence is false. The intended nondegenerate statement (divide by z², valid for C−D/2 ≠ 0) is never isolated in the source.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the nondegeneracy hypothesis (C,D) ≠ (0,0) (equivalently C ≠ D/2) to Lemma 3.1 and note that at that point G(z) → −5; a one-line change; all downstream uses, which employ C>0, are unaffected.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma 3.1 is an invalid statement as written (false at the single degenerate parameter point (C,D)=(0,0), where |G(∞)|=5>1). Every later use (the reduced G(z), Conclusion 3.3, the final scheme) operates with C≈0.019 ≠ 0, so no downstream guarantee is actually lost, but the lemma itself is false as stated.
issues.title: Lemma 3.1's iff condition fails at the degenerate parameter point (C,D)=(0,0)
issues.why_classification: A one-line local hypothesis (excluding the single degenerate parameter point) fully restores the lemma, and all downstream claims that use it operate in the nondegenerate regime, so every substantive guarantee survives.

issues.failure_explanation: From the quadratic z = [(1/3+13C) ± √((1/3+13C)²−24C)]/(6C), the source asserts 'So that the real part of z is (1/3+13C)/(6C)'. That is the real part only when the discriminant Δ = (1/3+13C)² − 24C is nonpositive. For every C < 0 one has Δ = (1/3+13C)² + 24|C| > 0, so both roots are real, and their product is 1/((3/2)C) = 2/(3C) < 0: exactly one root is negative. Hence, e.g., C = −0.05 gives roots ≈ −2.75 and +9.38, a pole of G in the closed left half-plane, contradicting the lemma's claim that for C < −1/39 'Re(z)>0'. The claimed equivalence is false on the entire branch C < 0; the correct statement is that G is analytic in the closed left half-plane iff C ≥ 0 (root z = 6 at C = 0).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the case analysis by: since Δ = (1/3+13C)² − 24C > 0 for all C < 0, the roots are real with product 2/(3C) < 0, so exactly one root is negative; therefore Lemma 3.2 should read 'analytic iff C ≥ 0' (the erroneous branch C < −1/39 is deleted). Contained, purely local correction; no downstream claim is affected.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma 3.2's stated equivalence is false on the entire asserted branch C < −1/39; Condition 1 (analyticity of G in the closed left half-plane) is mis-characterized there. The paper's subsequent A-stability range [0.018824, 0.045589] lies inside C > 0, where the corrected statement still holds, so that use is unaffected.
issues.title: Lemma 3.2's pole-location case analysis is wrong: the 'Re(z) = (1/3+13C)/(6C)' formula drops ±√Δ and is false for all C<0
issues.why_classification: The repair is a short local correction of a faulty case split (sign of the discriminant for C<0); the lemma's valid content (analyticity for C ≥ 0) and every downstream claim built on it are preserved unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Analytically proving $\lvert G(iy)\lvert\leq 1$ for all $y\in\mathbb{R}$ is complex. Instead, we employ a systematic numerical scanning algorithm to determine the A-stability conditions of the scheme.

The parameter space $C \in [0.00, 0.10]$ is discretized into 5,000 sampling points, while the frequency domain along the imaginary axis $y\in [10^{-8}, 10^{4}]$ is densely sampled using 25,000 logarithmically spaced points.
we derive the final form of this scheme, which is A-stable.
Furthermore, a sufficient condition for A-stability is established through systematic theoretical and numerical investigation

issues.failure_explanation: The Conclusion (and the surrounding prose, abstract, and Conclusions section) claims a theorem-level guarantee: the scheme 'achieves A-stability' for D=−C with C in the stated interval, quoting endpoints to six digits and calling C=0.018924 'optimal'. What the paper actually establishes is a finite grid scan: 5,000 sampled C-values in [0.00, 0.10] crossed with 25,000 sampled frequencies in y∈[10⁻⁸,10⁴], with no error bound. Condition 2, sup over the continuum y∈ℝ of |G(iy)| ≤ 1, is a statement about an interval of a real variable and a continuum of frequencies; a finite, truncated grid can neither certify |G(iy)| ≤ 1 off the grid (e.g., between samples or for |y|>10⁴) nor establish that the printed interval endpoints are the exact stability boundary. The paper's own text concedes the analytic verification was replaced by scanning ('Analytically proving |G(iy)|≤1 ... is complex. Instead, we employ a systematic numerical scanning algorithm'). The difference between what is claimed (a proven A-stability guarantee, an exact admissible interval, and a demonstrated optimal parameter) and what is established (numerical evidence on a discrete, truncated grid) is precisely a missing nontrivial analytic argument.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must rigorously prove sup over y∈ℝ of |G(iy)| ≤ 1 on a precisely characterized C-set (e.g., by reducing |G(iy)| ≤ 1 to a polynomial nonnegativity condition in y² for the explicit rational G(z) and verifying it by Sturm/root analysis), thereby also establishing exact endpoints, or else withdraw the A-stability guarantee and present the scan as numerical evidence only.
issues.overall_effect: The central advertised guarantee — A-stability of the final scheme (stage_1_final)-(Stage_2_final) with C ∈ [0.018824, 0.045589] and the 'optimal' C = 0.018924 — is unsupported as a mathematical result; the abstract's 'a sufficient condition for A-stability is established', the sentence 'we derive the final form of this scheme, which is A-stable', and the Conclusions' 'deriving the conditions under which A-stability can be achieved' all inherit the gap. The fourth-order accuracy derivation and the numerical experiments do not depend on it.
issues.title: A-stability of the Implicit TSFO scheme asserted as a conclusion but only supported by an uncontrolled numerical grid scan
issues.why_classification: No complete source-supported resolution exists: retaining the advertised A-stability guarantee requires a new nontrivial analytic proof absent from the paper, and any downgrade (e.g., 'numerically observed stability') abandons the paper's central advertised guarantee — both markers of a serious issue.
